claim: In glioma, microglia and infiltrating macrophages are exposed to factors that force them to produce cytokines and chemokines, which contribute to tumor growth and to maintaining a pro-tumorigenic, immunosuppressed microenvironment.
source: In glioma, microglia and infiltrating macrophages are exposed to factors that force them to produce cytokines and chemokines, which contribute to tumor growth and to maintaining a pro-tumorigenic, immunosuppressed microenvironment.
evidence: This is a general statement about glioma biology that draws from established scientific understanding of the tumor microenvironment.

claim: Housing glioma-bearing mice in enriched environment (EE) reverts the immunosuppressive phenotype of infiltrating myeloid cells, by modulating inflammatory gene expression.
source: We demonstrate that housing glioma-bearing mice in enriched environment (EE) reverts the immunosuppressive phenotype of infiltrating myeloid cells, by modulating inflammatory gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including RT-PCR analysis and gene expression profiling.

claim: Under enriched environment conditions, the branching and patrolling activity of myeloid cells is increased.
source: Under these conditions, the branching and patrolling activity of myeloid cells is increased, and their phagocytic activity is promoted.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis and two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Under enriched environment conditions, the phagocytic activity of myeloid cells is promoted.
source: Under these conditions, the branching and patrolling activity of myeloid cells is increased, and their phagocytic activity is promoted.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data showing increased phagocytic vacuoles in Figure 2i.

claim: Modulation of gene expression in myeloid cells depends on interferon-(IFN)-γ produced by natural killer (NK) cells.
source: Modulation of gene expression depends on interferon-(IFN)-γ produced by natural killer (NK) cells.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with NK cell depletion and IFN-γ blocking antibodies shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The modulation of myeloid cell gene expression disappears in mice depleted of NK cells.
source: This modulation disappears in mice depleted of NK cells or lacking IFN-γ, and was mimicked by exogenous interleukin-15 (IL-15).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR data in Figure 3a showing loss of gene expression changes after NK1.1 antibody treatment.

claim: The modulation of myeloid cell gene expression disappears in mice lacking IFN-γ.
source: This modulation disappears in mice depleted of NK cells or lacking IFN-γ, and was mimicked by exogenous interleukin-15 (IL-15).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR data in Figure 4b showing loss of gene expression changes after IFN-γ antibody treatment.

claim: Exogenous interleukin-15 (IL-15) mimics the effect of enriched environment on myeloid cell gene expression.
source: This modulation disappears in mice depleted of NK cells or lacking IFN-γ, and was mimicked by exogenous interleukin-15 (IL-15).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 5b showing that IL-15 infusion induces similar gene expression changes as EE.

claim: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) produced in the brain of mice housed in enriched environment mediates the expression of IL-15 in CD11b+ cells.
source: Further, we describe a key role for brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) that is produced in the brain of mice housed in EE, in mediating the expression of IL-15 in CD11b+ cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5g-i showing BDNF infusion increases IL-15 expression and Bdnf+/- mice lack this increase.

claim: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a grade IV (WHO) brain tumor.
source: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a grade IV (WHO) brain tumor, characterized by high cell proliferation, active angiogenesis and invasion capability.
evidence: This is established medical classification knowledge.

claim: Glioblastoma is characterized by high cell proliferation, active angiogenesis and invasion capability.
source: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a grade IV (WHO) brain tumor, characterized by high cell proliferation, active angiogenesis and invasion capability.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GBM characteristics.

claim: Glioma-associated myeloid cells (GAMs) comprise microglia, peripheral monocytes, perivascular macrophages and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC).
source: The latter population comprises microglia, peripheral monocytes, perivascular macrophages and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC) (Quail and Joyce, 2017), and may represent up to 30% of total tumor mass (Graeber et al., 2002; Markovic et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Glioma-associated myeloid cells may represent up to 30% of total tumor mass.
source: The latter population comprises microglia, peripheral monocytes, perivascular macrophages and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC) (Quail and Joyce, 2017), and may represent up to 30% of total tumor mass (Graeber et al., 2002; Markovic et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Graeber et al., 2002 and Markovic et al., 2009.

claim: GAMs play an active part in the enhancement of the invasive and proliferative properties of GBM.
source: GAMs play an active part in the enhancement of the invasive and proliferative properties of GBM, further contributing to the immunosuppressive phenotype of the tumor microenvironment (Markovic et al., 2005; Coniglio and Segall, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: GAMs contribute to the immunosuppressive phenotype of the tumor microenvironment.
source: GAMs play an active part in the enhancement of the invasive and proliferative properties of GBM, further contributing to the immunosuppressive phenotype of the tumor microenvironment (Markovic et al., 2005; Coniglio and Segall, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Murine GAMs express several genes that have anti-inflammatory properties.
source: Murine GAMs express several genes that have anti-inflammatory properties, and many efforts aim to promote the expression of pro-inflammatory genes by GAMs, as this phenotype is associated with better patient prognosis and increased survival in animal models (Pyonteck et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pyonteck et al., 2013.

claim: Pro-inflammatory phenotype of GAMs is associated with better patient prognosis and increased survival in animal models.
source: Murine GAMs express several genes that have anti-inflammatory properties, and many efforts aim to promote the expression of pro-inflammatory genes by GAMs, as this phenotype is associated with better patient prognosis and increased survival in animal models (Pyonteck et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pyonteck et al., 2013.

claim: Factors involved in chronic inflammation may increase the incidence of several tumor types.
source: However, epidemiological studies have demonstrated that factors involved in chronic inflammation may increase the incidence of several tumor types (Mantovani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mantovani et al., 2008.

claim: Environmental stimuli have been shown to shape brain functions, modulating plasticity and learning and memory functions.
source: Environmental stimuli have been shown to shape brain functions, modulating plasticity and learning and memory functions, and reducing the impact of neurodegenerative diseases in animal models and in patients (Sale et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sale et al., 2014.

claim: Environmental stimuli reduce the impact of neurodegenerative diseases in animal models and in patients.
source: Environmental stimuli have been shown to shape brain functions, modulating plasticity and learning and memory functions, and reducing the impact of neurodegenerative diseases in animal models and in patients (Sale et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sale et al., 2014.

claim: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a key cerebral mediator of environmental enrichment effects on brain function.
source: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a key cerebral mediator of these phenomena (Branchi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Branchi et al., 2004.

claim: Housing mice in an enriched environment reduced intracranial glioma growth through indirect mechanisms acting through innate immune natural killer (NK) cells.
source: We have previously demonstrated that housing mice in an enriched environment (EE) reduced intracranial glioma growth, with indirect mechanisms acting through innate immune natural killer (NK) cells, and with direct effects of BDNF on the truncated isoform 1 of the tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkBT1), which is expressed by tumor cells.
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors, likely Garofalo et al., 2015.

claim: BDNF has direct effects on the truncated isoform 1 of the tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkBT1), which is expressed by tumor cells.
source: We have previously demonstrated that housing mice in an enriched environment (EE) reduced intracranial glioma growth, with indirect mechanisms acting through innate immune natural killer (NK) cells, and with direct effects of BDNF on the truncated isoform 1 of the tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkBT1), which is expressed by tumor cells.
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: Anti-tumor activity of an enriched environment has been shown in different cancers.
source: Anti-tumor activity of an EE has been shown in different cancers (Cao et al., 2010; Nachat-Kappes et al., 2012; Garofalo et al., 2015), even if some results were not confirmed (Westwood et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Some studies did not confirm the anti-tumor activity of enriched environment.
source: Anti-tumor activity of an EE has been shown in different cancers (Cao et al., 2010; Nachat-Kappes et al., 2012; Garofalo et al., 2015), even if some results were not confirmed (Westwood et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Westwood et al., 2013.

claim: Environmental stimuli shape immune functions, modulating NK cells.
source: Environmental stimuli also shape immune functions, modulating NK cells (Garofalo et al., 2015; Song et al., 2017), T helper cells (Rattazzi et al., 2016), and myeloid cells (Chabry et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Environmental stimuli shape immune functions, modulating T helper cells.
source: Environmental stimuli also shape immune functions, modulating NK cells (Garofalo et al., 2015; Song et al., 2017), T helper cells (Rattazzi et al., 2016), and myeloid cells (Chabry et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rattazzi et al., 2016.

claim: Environmental stimuli shape immune functions, modulating myeloid cells.
source: Environmental stimuli also shape immune functions, modulating NK cells (Garofalo et al., 2015; Song et al., 2017), T helper cells (Rattazzi et al., 2016), and myeloid cells (Chabry et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chabry et al., 2015.

claim: NK cells exert anti-tumor function by direct cytotoxic activity, producing several cytokines, chemokines and growth factors.
source: NK cells exert anti-tumor function by direct cytotoxic activity, producing several cytokines, chemokines and growth factors (Vivier et al., 2011; Guillerey and Smyth, 2016; Stabile et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IFN-γ contributes to tumor immune-surveillance and interacts with T cells, dendritic cells and monocytes.
source: Among the cytokines, interferon (IFN)-γ contributes to tumor immune-surveillance and interacts with T cells, dendritic cells and monocytes (Kaplan et al., 1998; Dunn et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kaplan et al., 1998 and Dunn et al., 2006.

claim: IFN-γ is a pleiotropic cytokine, which has anti-tumor activity in different neoplasms by inhibiting cell proliferation and exerting anti-angiogenic activity.
source: IFN-γ is a pleiotropic cytokine, which has anti-tumor activity in different neoplasms by inhibiting cell proliferation and exerting anti-angiogenic activity (Parker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Parker et al., 2016.

claim: IFN-γ counters the acquisition of a pro-tumor phenotype by GAMs and reverses the immunosuppressive phenotype.
source: In particular, IFN-γ counters the acquisition of a pro-tumor phenotype by GAMs and reverses the immunosuppressive phenotype (Duluc et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duluc et al., 2009.

claim: The maturation and survival of NK cells require IL-15.
source: The maturation and survival of NK cells require IL-15, which also stimulates IFN-γ production (Yu et al., 2006), and mice lacking IL-15 or one of its signaling components are devoid of NK cells (Koka et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yu et al., 2006 and Koka et al., 2003.

claim: IL-15 stimulates IFN-γ production by NK cells.
source: The maturation and survival of NK cells require IL-15, which also stimulates IFN-γ production (Yu et al., 2006), and mice lacking IL-15 or one of its signaling components are devoid of NK cells (Koka et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2006.

claim: Mice lacking IL-15 or one of its signaling components are devoid of NK cells.
source: The maturation and survival of NK cells require IL-15, which also stimulates IFN-γ production (Yu et al., 2006), and mice lacking IL-15 or one of its signaling components are devoid of NK cells (Koka et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koka et al., 2003.

claim: CD11b+ cells from the ipsilateral hemisphere of SE mice preferentially express anti-inflammatory markers including Chil3, Mrc1, Arg1 and Retnla compared to those from the contralateral hemisphere.
source: RT-PCR analysis revealed that CD11b+ cells from the ILH (compared to those from the CLH) of mice housed in SE (SE mice) preferentially express anti-inflammatory markers that include Chil3, Mrc1, Arg1 and Retnla (Gabrusiewicz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Some pro-inflammatory genes, like Tnfa and Nos2, were upregulated in the ipsilateral hemisphere of SE mice.
source: Some pro-inflammatory genes, like Tnfa and Nos2, were also upregulated in the ILH, whereas no differences were observed for Cd86 and Il1b.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: No differences were observed for Cd86 and Il1b expression between ipsilateral and contralateral hemispheres in SE mice.
source: Some pro-inflammatory genes, like Tnfa and Nos2, were also upregulated in the ILH, whereas no differences were observed for Cd86 and Il1b.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: In EE, the gene expression of CD11b+ cells isolated from the ipsilateral hemisphere was deeply modified, showing significant increase of pro-inflammatory and reduction of anti-inflammatory genes.
source: In EE, the gene expression of CD11b+ cells isolated from the ILH was deeply modified, showing the significant increase of pro-inflammatory and reduction of anti-inflammatory genes (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Tumor size was significantly reduced in EE mice compared to SE mice in CT-2a glioma model.
source: Also in this condition, tumor size was significantly reduced in EE mice as compared to SE mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is supported by tumor volume measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: In EE mice, the expression of anti-inflammatory genes was reduced in both microglia and infiltrating monocytes.
source: In the ILH of EE mice, the expression of anti-inflammatory genes was reduced in both microglia and infiltrating monocytes, whereas the expression of anti-tumor, pro-inflammatory genes was increased only in microglia (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1b,c.

claim: In EE mice, the expression of anti-tumor, pro-inflammatory genes was increased only in microglia, not in infiltrating monocytes.
source: In the ILH of EE mice, the expression of anti-inflammatory genes was reduced in both microglia and infiltrating monocytes, whereas the expression of anti-tumor, pro-inflammatory genes was increased only in microglia (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1b,c.

claim: Genes that were upregulated in microglia from the ipsilateral hemisphere of EE mice were enriched in Gene Ontology terms such as 'response to interferon-gamma' and 'innate immune response'.
source: Genes that were upregulated in microglia from the ILH of EE mice were enriched in Gene Ontology (GO) terms such as 'response to interferon-gamma' and 'innate immune response' (Figure 1d,e).
evidence: This is supported by microarray and GO analysis data shown in Figure 1d,e.

claim: Only GFP+ cells in the ipsilateral hemisphere have outward-rectifying potassium currents (Kor), which are absent in the contralateral hemisphere.
source: As shown in Figure 2a, only GFP+ cells in the ILH have outward-rectifying potassium currents (Kor, flowing through Kv1.3 and Kv1.5), which are absent in the CLH, and the average current amplitude is not modified by exposure to EE.
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The average amplitude of outward-rectifying potassium currents is not modified by exposure to EE.
source: As shown in Figure 2a, only GFP+ cells in the ILH have outward-rectifying potassium currents (Kor, flowing through Kv1.3 and Kv1.5), which are absent in the CLH, and the average current amplitude is not modified by exposure to EE.
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: In the peritumoral region, the occurrence of Kor currents is increased by EE.
source: Focusing on the peritumoral region, the occurrence of Kor currents is increased by EE (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: In the contralateral hemisphere, the amplitude of the inward-rectifying K currents (Kir) is increased in the GFP+ cells of EE mice.
source: In the CLH, the amplitude of the inward-rectifying K currents (Kir, carried by Kv2.1 channels) is increased in the GFP+ cells of EE mice (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: In the peritumoral region of EE mice, GFP+ cells have an increased number and length of branches, and cover a wider parenchymal region.
source: Our data show that, in the peritumoral region of EE mice, GFP+ cells have an increased number and length of branches, and cover a wider parenchymal region (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 2d.

claim: GFP+ cells in the peritumoral region of EE mice display a reduced patrolling activity, as indicated by reduced velocity and process extension into the brain parenchyma.
source: On the other hand, these cells display a reduced patrolling activity, as indicated by reduced velocity and process extension into the brain parenchyma (Figure 2e), which is probably balanced by their wider coverage (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Only GFP+ cells in the peritumoral area rearrange their processes toward a pipette-guided focal application of ATP.
source: We also observed that only GFP+ cells in the peritumoral area rearrange their processes toward a pipette-guided focal application of ATP.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The speed of ATP-directed process movements increases in EE.
source: The speed of these movements increases in EE (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: CD11b+ cells isolated from the brain of EE mice have increased expression of P2RY12.
source: This behavior could be due to an increased expression of P2RY12 (Figure 2g) in CD11b+ cells isolated from the brain of EE mice.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: In EE mice, GFP+ cells inside the tumor have increased process length and total surface area.
source: Two-photon analysis shows that in EE mice, GFP+ cells inside the tumor have increased process length and total surface area (Figure 2h).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: In EE mice, IBA1+ cells inside the tumor have reduced cell body roundness, indicating ramified (versus amoeboid) morphologies.
source: Electron microscopy showed ultrastructural differences too: in EE mice, IBA1+ cells inside the tumor have reduced cell body roundness, indicating ramified (versus amoeboid) morphologies, as well as reduced solidity, being delineated by smoother plasma membranes (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: In EE mice, IBA1+ cells inside the tumor have reduced solidity, being delineated by smoother plasma membranes.
source: Electron microscopy showed ultrastructural differences too: in EE mice, IBA1+ cells inside the tumor have reduced cell body roundness, indicating ramified (versus amoeboid) morphologies, as well as reduced solidity, being delineated by smoother plasma membranes (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: In EE mice, microglia contained an increased number of phagocytic vacuoles, sometimes with cellular elements showing signs of digestion.
source: They also contained an increased number of phagocytic vacuoles, sometimes with cellular elements showing signs of digestion.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: In SE, NK cell depletion per se modifies the phenotype of CD11b+ cells in tumor-bearing brains towards an anti-inflammatory phenotype.
source: In SE, NK cell depletion per se modifies the phenotype of CD11b+ cells in tumor-bearing brains towards an anti-inflammatory phenotype (Figure 3a; note that the scale values differ from those in Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: In EE mice with glioma, NK cell depletion blocks CD11b+ cell polarization towards a pro-inflammatory phenotype.
source: In EE mice with glioma, NK cell depletion blocks CD11b+ cell polarization towards a pro-inflammatory phenotype, demonstrating the importance of NK-CD11b+ intercellular communication for these effects.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: In the EE condition, the frequency of direct contacts between NK cells and glioma cells was significantly increased.
source: On the other hand, in EE conditions, the frequency of direct contacts between NK cells and glioma cells was significantly increased (Figure 3b), suggesting that these structural interactions underlie the increased NK cell degranulation (see below).
evidence: This is supported by 3D reconstruction and distance analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In EE mice, IBA1+ cells with the ultrastructural characteristics of microglia and juxtaposed to NK cells contain an increased number of phagocytic vacuoles.
source: Electron microscopic analysis of tumors (Figure 3c) further shows that in EE mice, IBA1+ cells with the ultrastructural characteristics of microglia (Tremblay et al., 2012) and juxtaposed to NK cells contain an increased number of phagocytic vacuoles, sometimes containing cellular elements in the process of being digested.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: In the brain of EE mice, there is an increased frequency of NK cells expressing granzyme B and IFN-γ.
source: We confirmed (Garofalo et al., 2015) that in the brain of EE mice, there is an increased frequency of NK cells expressing granzyme B and IFN-γ (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), and this leads to an increased degranulation of NK cells ex vivo (not shown) which was further increased when challenged against tumor cells (GL261 and YAC-1 cells, Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Increased frequency of granzyme B and IFN-γ expressing NK cells leads to increased degranulation of NK cells ex vivo.
source: We confirmed (Garofalo et al., 2015) that in the brain of EE mice, there is an increased frequency of NK cells expressing granzyme B and IFN-γ (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), and this leads to an increased degranulation of NK cells ex vivo (not shown) which was further increased when challenged against tumor cells (GL261 and YAC-1 cells, Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by degranulation assay data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: NK cells were more distant from CD31+ endothelial cells in EE condition, probably because of an increased colonization of the brain parenchyma.
source: NK cells were also more distant from CD31+ endothelial cells, probably because of an increased colonization of the brain parenchyma in the EE condition (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and distance analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Glioma-bearing EE mice express higher levels of IFN-γ in the ipsilateral hemisphere.
source: Investigating the potential role of IFN-γ as mediator of NK-cell-mediated effect, we demonstrated that glioma-bearing EE mice express higher levels of IFN-γ in the ILH, and that NK cell depletion abolishes this increase (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: NK cell depletion abolishes the increase of IFN-γ in the ipsilateral hemisphere of EE mice.
source: Investigating the potential role of IFN-γ as mediator of NK-cell-mediated effect, we demonstrated that glioma-bearing EE mice express higher levels of IFN-γ in the ILH, and that NK cell depletion abolishes this increase (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: IFN-γ depletion completely abolishes the effect of EE on CD11b+ cell phenotypic changes.
source: IFN-γ depletion completely abolishes the effect of EE on CD11b+ cell phenotypic changes (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: IFN-γ depletion reduces the effect of EE on tumor volume.
source: This treatment has consequences similar to those of NK cell depletion (Garofalo et al., 2015), reducing the effect of EE on tumor volume and inhibiting the pro-survival effect (Figure 4c–d).
evidence: This is supported by tumor volume measurements shown in Figure 4c.

claim: IFN-γ depletion inhibits the pro-survival effect of EE.
source: This treatment has consequences similar to those of NK cell depletion (Garofalo et al., 2015), reducing the effect of EE on tumor volume and inhibiting the pro-survival effect (Figure 4c–d).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: EE housing reduces the extent of CD31 staining, probably because of the production of angiostatic chemokines.
source: EE and IFN-γ depletion alone have opposite effects on angiogenesis. EE housing reduces the extent of CD31 staining, probably because of the production of angiostatic chemokines (Coughlin et al., 1998); whereas IFN-γ depletion per se increases angiogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4e and citation to Coughlin et al., 1998.

claim: IFN-γ depletion per se increases angiogenesis.
source: EE and IFN-γ depletion alone have opposite effects on angiogenesis. EE housing reduces the extent of CD31 staining, probably because of the production of angiostatic chemokines (Coughlin et al., 1998); whereas IFN-γ depletion per se increases angiogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The blunted effect of EE on tumor size reduction in IFN-γ-depleted mice was at least partially dependent on a reduced inhibition of tumor cell proliferation.
source: The blunted effect of EE on tumor size reduction was at least partially dependent on a reduced inhibition of tumor cell proliferation, as more Ki67+ cells were present in the tumor mass of IFN-γ-depleted mice (Figure 4f), in accordance with the anti-proliferative activity of IFN-γ.
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: IFN-γ treatment decreases expression of the human anti-inflammatory genes Cd163, Mmp12 and Tgfb in CD11b+ cells from human GBM tissues.
source: Figure 4g shows that IFN-γ treatment decreases expression of the human anti-inflammatory genes Cd163, Mmp12 and Tgfb, and increases expression of the pro-inflammatory genes Il12a, Nos2 and Cxcl10.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data from human GBM samples shown in Figure 4g.

claim: IFN-γ treatment increases expression of the pro-inflammatory genes Il12a, Nos2 and Cxcl10 in CD11b+ cells from human GBM tissues.
source: Figure 4g shows that IFN-γ treatment decreases expression of the human anti-inflammatory genes Cd163, Mmp12 and Tgfb, and increases expression of the pro-inflammatory genes Il12a, Nos2 and Cxcl10.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data from human GBM samples shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Brain infusion of IL-15 increased the frequency of infiltrating NK cells in the ipsilateral hemisphere.
source: We then investigated the effect of IL-15 on myeloid cell phenotype. CD11b+ cells isolated from the brains of glioma-bearing mice treated with IL-15, as described in the scheme of Figure 5a, showed a phenotype shifted towards the pro-inflammatory state, with significantly increased expression of pro- and reduced expression of anti-inflammatory genes (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: CD11b+ cells isolated from the brains of glioma-bearing mice treated with IL-15 showed a phenotype shifted towards the pro-inflammatory state.
source: We then investigated the effect of IL-15 on myeloid cell phenotype. CD11b+ cells isolated from the brains of glioma-bearing mice treated with IL-15, as described in the scheme of Figure 5a, showed a phenotype shifted towards the pro-inflammatory state, with significantly increased expression of pro- and reduced expression of anti-inflammatory genes (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: IL-15 treatment reduced the amount of CD68+ and F4/80+/CD68+ cells in the tumor mass.
source: In accordance with this modulation of gene expression, IL-15 treatment also reduced the amount of CD68+ and F4/80+/CD68+ cells in the tumor mass (Figure 5c), indicative of reduced activation of GAMs.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The IL-15-dependent modulation of gene expression was completely absent in glioma-bearing mice in which NK cells were depleted.
source: Interestingly, the IL-15-dependent modulation of gene expression was completely absent in glioma-bearing mice in which NK cells were depleted (Figure 5d), further supporting the hypothesis that IL-15 modulates CD11b+ cell phenotype by acting through NK cells.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: In Il15ra–/– mice, tumor size was increased in SE, and there was a smaller effect of reducing tumor size in EE.
source: The role of IL-15 in modulating the effect of EE was also confirmed with glioma Il15ra–/– mice: in these animals, we observed increased tumor size in SE, and a smaller effect of reducing tumor size in EE (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is supported by tumor volume measurements shown in Figure 5e.

claim: In CD11b+ cells isolated from the brain of Il15ra–/– mice, the modulation of gene expression induced by EE was fully abolished.
source: In addition, in CD11b+ cells isolated from the brain of Il15ra–/– mice, the modulation of gene expression induced by EE was fully abolished (Figure 5f), thus demonstrating a key role for IL-15 signaling in modulating GAMs' phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The infusion of BDNF in mouse brain induces IL-15 production by CD11b+ cells.
source: We investigated the possible effects of BDNF on glioma biology, demonstrating that the infusion of BDNF in mouse brain induces IL-15 production by CD11b+ cells (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5g.

claim: Bdnf+/- EE mice have no increased production of IL-15 in CD11b+ cells.
source: In line with the hypothesis that BDNF is a key neurotrophin in mediating the effects of EE, we observed that Bdnf -/+ EE mice have no increased production of IL-15 in CD11b+ cells (Figure 5h).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5h.

claim: BDNF induced IL-15 production by microglia only upon treatment with IL-4 or co-culture with glioma cells.
source: We also analyzed BDNF-induced IL-15 expression in vitro, using primary microglial cell cultures obtained after stimulation with vehicle, with LPS + IFN-γ or with IL-4, or co-cultured with GBM. We observed that BDNF induced IL-15 production by microglia only upon treatment with IL-4 or co-culture with glioma cells (Figure 5i).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5i.

claim: There is a reduction in the frequency of CD11b+/Ly6c+ cells expressed as a percentage of infiltrating CD45+ cells in the brain of EE mice.
source: We report a reduction in the frequency of CD11b+/Ly6c+ cells expressed as a percentage of infiltrating CD45+ cells in the brain of EE mice (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: In SE, the CD11b+ cells extracted from the ipsilateral hemisphere of clodronate-treated mice expressed all the anti-inflammatory markers analyzed except for CD206.
source: In these mice, the housing conditions induced a minor variation of gene expression: in particular, in SE, the CD11b+ cells extracted from the ILH expressed all the anti-inflammatory markers analyzed except for CD206 (consistent with a selective peripheral phagocyte depletion).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: In EE clodronate-treated mice, there was a general decrease of anti-inflammatory genes accompanied by a significant increase of pro-inflammatory genes.
source: In EE mice, we observed a general decrease of anti-inflammatory genes accompanied by a significant increase of pro-inflammatory genes (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: In clodronate-treated animals, even in SE, tumor size is reduced.
